Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
try hard not think about the trauma
I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

vignette:
Daniel Mercer, a 36-year-old White American man, came to treatment after months of telling himself that what happened was either unreal or "not even as bad as people make it sound." He said this in a flat, practiced way, as if repeating a line he had used to get through workdays and family dinners, but the strain showed when he tried to describe the disaster itself. Daniel had been caught in a man-made catastrophe in a crowded public setting, where people surged against one another in panic and he found himself pressed so tightly among bodies that he could barely move. What stayed with him most were not long, coherent memories but a handful of sharply lit images: a stranger's face twisted in alarm inches from his own, the crush of people forcing forward despite others falling or pleading, and the feel of a particular rough synthetic surface under his hands as he tried to brace himself. Those moments sat in his mind like still photographs, disconnected from everything before and after, yet somehow more vivid than the rest of his life.

When he recalled the event, shame came immediately. He did not describe this as embarrassment so much as a sick, engulfing sense that something about him had been exposed. He was ashamed of what he remembered seeing in himself during those seconds and ashamed, too, of how helpless he had been in the middle of other people's selfishness and disorder. What troubled him deeply was the memory of people shoving, ignoring one another, acting as if basic decency had vanished. He had come away convinced that when people misbehave in public-cutting lines, yelling at staff, pushing past others-something dangerous is close at hand. Since the disaster, small scenes that other people shrugged off could jolt him: a customer at the store where he worked leaning over the counter and speaking aggressively, two shoppers arguing in an aisle, someone crowding too close behind him while he was stocking shelves. In those moments Daniel's attention narrowed and his body reacted before he had words for it. He was not thinking abstractly about trauma; he was back in the felt certainty that people stop caring and things turn bad fast.

His work in retail made this hard to escape. The sales floor was full of exactly the kind of physical proximity he now dreaded. Customers brushed past him in narrow aisles, stood shoulder to shoulder during promotions, and sometimes shoved carts carelessly. Even handling certain merchandise could unsettle him if the texture matched what his hands had met during the disaster. He noticed himself freezing for a beat when his fingers touched that material, then forcing himself to continue while trying not to let anyone see his reaction. He began trading tasks with coworkers to avoid crowded sections of the store and timed his breaks to stay away from peak foot traffic. At home, he was less willing to go to busy places with his wife, and she had started to notice how often he scanned rooms, repositioned himself near exits, or refused plans without giving a real explanation.

Daniel fought his mind constantly. If an image broke through, he pushed it down hard and tried to think of anything else. He avoided news coverage, conversations about disasters, and even ordinary moments of reflection because he feared the pictures would come back with full force. When suppression failed, he sometimes hurt himself physically in small, private ways to interrupt the flood of memory-something sharp, immediate, and concrete that could pull him away from the images. He described this matter-of-factly, not as a wish to die, but as a desperate attempt to stop the internal replay. The replay itself felt unbearable because the remembered fragments were so intense and sensory, more real than everyday experience, as if the event had greater solidity than the room he was currently standing in.

Over time, the costs accumulated. At work he became known as tense with difficult customers and unreliable during busy sales periods. At home he grew more withdrawn, especially when his wife challenged his insistence that he was fine. What finally brought him in was not a single collapse but the recognition that the effort of denying, suppressing, and physically interrupting his own mind was no longer holding. After a recent shift in which an argument between customers and the press of bodies near the registers left him shaken for hours, he went home and admitted that he was afraid of what happened in his head when reminders got too close. Sitting in treatment, Daniel seemed caught between two wishes: to make the whole thing smaller, less real, and to find some way to remember it without being swallowed by shame.
